question: The University of Cagliari has stated that, under the 2026-2027 Erasmus+ mobility scheme, participating students will, in addition to their travel grant, receive an additional top-up if they choose means of transport that have a low environmental impact. The University has specifically excluded planes and ships from this category.

There are concerns that this policy is not fair towards students based in island regions, who need to use these modes of transport as a matter of geographical necessity. These candidates are, as a result, less likely to obtain the top-up compared to those who can use road or rail to reach their intended destinations.

This Erasmus+ sustainable mobility drive should include guarantees that all participants enjoy equal access to the programme, and should therefore take the specific characteristics of island regions into account. In the light of the above, I ask the Commission: 1.

What are the European criteria that regulate the Erasmus+ sustainable travel top-up, and under what conditions can students from Sardinia, Sicily and other islands who combine air or sea travel with low-emission modes of transport qualify for this grant?

Will it introduce specific measures or additional funding for island-based Erasmus+ candidates with a view to ensuring that this cohort is not put at an economic disadvantage because of its limited transport options?
